title: No part of Scripture is superfluous
english: I imagine many of you are puzzled by this passage from the apostolic reading, or rather consider this part of the letter a side matter and superfluous, because it contains only greetings, one after another in quick succession. That is why I myself, though I had set out today in another direction, have left that subject and am preparing to come down to this one, so that you may learn that in the divine Scriptures nothing is superfluous, nothing is a side matter—not one iota, not one stroke—but even a bare greeting opens a vast sea of meaning for us. And why do I say a bare greeting? Often the addition of a single letter has brought in the full force of whole thoughts. You can see this in the naming of Abraham. How absurd it would be, when you receive a letter from a friend, not to read only the body of the letter but also the greeting written at the bottom, and from that especially to infer the disposition of the writer—yet when Paul writes, or rather not Paul, but the grace of the Spirit dictating the letter to a whole city and so great a people, and through them to the entire world, to think that anything in it is superfluous, and to pass over it lightly, and not to consider that these attitudes have turned everything upside down? This is what has filled us with so much carelessness: that we do not go through all the Scriptures, but choose what we think is clearer and pay no attention to the rest. This is what has introduced heresies: the unwillingness to go through the whole body, the belief that something is superfluous and a side matter. That is why we have been diligent about everything else—not only the superfluous things, but even the useless and harmful ones—while skill in the Scriptures has been neglected and despised. Those who are excited about watching horse races can tell you with complete accuracy the names, the herd, the breed, the homeland, and the upbringing of the horses, and their years of life, and their performances in races, and which horse paired with which will seize the victory, and which horse released from which starting gate, and with which charioteer, will win the race and outrun its rival. And those who spend their time around the orchestra show no less madness than these—indeed even more—about those who disgrace themselves in the theaters, I mean the mimes and dancers, recounting their family, homeland, upbringing, and everything else. But when we are asked how many letters of Paul there are and which they are, we cannot even state the number. And if some do know the number, when asked about the cities that received the letters, they are at a loss to answer. A eunuch, a barbarian, pulled in ten thousand directions by ten thousand concerns, was so devoted to books that he did not rest even during his journey, but seated on his carriage he applied himself with great care to the reading of the divine Scriptures. Yet we, who do not have even the smallest fraction of his business, are strangers even to the names of the letters—and this though we gather here every Lord's day and enjoy listening to the divine Scriptures.
orientation: Chrysostom opens his homily on Paul's greeting to Priscilla and Aquila by addressing his congregation about their neglect of Scripture's seemingly minor parts.

title: The greeting to Priscilla and Aquila is not superfluous
english: But so that we do not spend the whole discourse only on rebuke, come, let us bring forward the greeting itself—the one that seems superfluous and intrusive. For when it is unfolded and the gain it offers to those who attend to it with care is shown, then the accusation against those who neglect such treasures and throw spiritual wealth out of their hands will be all the greater. What then is the greeting? “Greet Priscilla and Aquila,” he says, “my coworkers in the Lord” (Romans 16:3). Does it not seem to be a bare greeting, showing us nothing great or noble? Come then, let us spend the entire discussion on this one greeting alone. Or rather, we will not even be able today to draw up for you all the thoughts contained in these few words, even if we try hard; the abundance of contemplations born from this short greeting will have to be stored up for another day. For I am not preparing to go through all of it, but only a part, a beginning and preface: “Greet Priscilla and Aquila.”

First, one must be astonished at Paul’s virtue: he had been entrusted with the whole inhabited world, land and sea, all the cities under the sun, barbarians and Greeks, and he carried so many peoples within himself—yet he showed such care for one man and one woman. And second, one must marvel at this: how wakeful and attentive his soul was, remembering not only all people in common but also each of the approved and noble ones individually. For now it is no wonder that those who preside over the churches do this, since those disturbances have been calmed and they have taken on the care of only one city. But then, not only the greatness of the dangers, but also the length of the journey, the multitude of cares, the waves crashing one after another, the fact that he could not always be present with everyone continually, and many other things besides—these were enough to drive out of memory even very close friends. But they did not drive these two out. How then were they not driven out? Because of Paul’s greatness of soul and his warm and genuine love. For he held them in his mind so firmly that he remembered them often even in his letters.

But let us see who these people were and what kind of people they were, who so captured Paul and drew him to their own affection. Were they consuls and generals and prefects? Did they possess some other distinction, or were they clothed in great wealth, among those who led the city? None of these things can be said. Quite the opposite: they were poor and needy, living from the work of their hands. For they were, he says, tentmakers by trade (Acts 18:3). And Paul was not ashamed, nor did he consider it a reproach to a most imperial city and a proud people to command them to greet those craftsmen. Nor did he think he was insulting them by his friendship with those people—so thoroughly had he taught everyone then to practice discipline. Yet we, who often have relatives who are somewhat poorer, estrange ourselves from closeness with them and consider it a reproach if we are ever discovered to be related to them. But Paul was not like that. Instead, he prides himself on the matter, and he made it clear not only to those of his own time but to all who came after that those tentmakers held the first place in his friendship.
orientation: Chrysostom is preaching on Romans 16:3, where Paul sends greetings to Priscilla and Aquila, and he is about to show that even this brief greeting contains great treasure.

title: True nobility is virtue, not ancestry; marriage and work are no obstacle
english: And let no one say to me, “What is so great and wonderful about a man who came from the same trade not being ashamed of his fellow craftsmen?” What are you saying? This very thing is the greatest and most wonderful of all. For those who can point to the splendor of their ancestors are not as ashamed of their inferiors as those who once lived in the same lowliness and then suddenly rose to some brilliance and splendor. And that nothing was more brilliant or more splendid than Paul—that he was even more distinguished than kings themselves—is surely clear to everyone. For the man who commanded demons, raised the dead, and by a command could both blind and heal the blinded, whose garments and shadows dissolved every kind of disease, was clearly no longer considered a mere human being, but some angel descended from heaven. Yet although he enjoyed such glory and was admired everywhere, and wherever he appeared drew everyone to himself, he was not ashamed of the tentmaker, nor did he think that those holding such great dignities were being diminished. For it is likely that in the church of the Romans there were many distinguished people, whom he compelled to greet those poor ones. For he knew—he knew clearly—that nobility is not made by splendor of wealth or abundance of possessions, but by gentleness of character. Those who are deprived of this and pride themselves on the glory of those who bore them adorn themselves with a bare name of nobility, not with the reality. Or rather, the name itself is often exposed if one goes back to the earlier ancestors of these noble people. For if you examine with precision the distinguished and brilliant man who has a famous father and grandfather, you will often find that his great-grandfather was some lowly and nameless person. And likewise, if we go up through the whole lineage of those who seem lowly and investigate it little by little, we will often find that their earlier ancestors were prefects and generals, and one might find that they had become horse-keepers and swineherds. Paul knew all these things, and so he made no great account of them, but sought nobility of soul, and taught others to admire it. This, then, is no small fruit we gather from this passage: not to be ashamed of any of the lowlier ones, to seek virtue of soul, and to consider all the external things that surround us as superfluous and useless.

There is also another gain, no less than this one, that we can harvest from here—one that, when put into practice, most of all holds our life together. What is this? Not to accuse marriage, and not to think that having a wife, raising children, managing a household, and practicing a trade is a hindrance and obstacle to the road that leads to virtue. Look, here there were a man and a woman, and they managed workshops and practiced a trade, and they displayed a discipline far more exact than those living in monasteries. How is this clear? From what Paul called them—or rather, not only from what he called them, but also from what he testified about them afterward. For after saying, “Greet Priscilla and Aquila” (Romans 16:3), he added their dignity. What dignity was that? He did not say “the rich,” “the distinguished,” “the well-born.” But what? “My coworkers in the Lord.” Nothing could equal this as an account of virtue. And not only from this, but also from the fact that he stayed with them—not for one day, or two or three, but for two whole years—one can see their virtue.
orientation: Chrysostom is preaching on Romans 16:3, where Paul greets Priscilla and Aquila, and is now answering an imagined objection that Paul's lack of shame toward fellow tentmakers was nothing remarkable.

title: The apostles sought worthy souls, not fine houses
english: Just as the rulers of those outside would never choose to be lodged with cheap and humble people, but seek splendid houses belonging to men of note, so that the meanness of their hosts may not damage the greatness of their dignity, so the apostles did the same. They did not lodge with just anyone, but just as those rulers sought splendor of house, these sought virtue of soul, and after examining thoroughly who was suitable for them, they lodged with those people. For a law from Christ lay down this command. “Whatever city or house you enter,” he says, “ask who in it is worthy, and stay there” (Matthew 10:11). So these two were worthy of Paul; and if worthy of Paul, they were worthy of the angels. I would confidently call that little room both heaven and a church. For where Paul was, there Christ was. “If you seek proof,” he says, “of Christ speaking in me” (2 Corinthians 13:3). And where Christ was, there angels continually came and went. And think what sort of people they became who even before this had shown themselves worthy of serving Paul, living with him for two years and observing closely his bearing, his walk, his gaze, his manner of dress, his comings and goings, and everything else. For with the saints, not only their words, not only their teachings and exhortations, but the whole rest of their conduct is enough to be a teaching of discipline for those who pay attention. Think how great a thing it was to see Paul dining, rebuking, encouraging, praying, weeping, going out and coming in. If we, having only fourteen letters, carry them around everywhere in the world, what would those people not have become who had the source of the letters, the tongue of the world, the light of the churches, the foundation of the faith, the pillar and support of the truth, living with such an angel? For if his garments were fearsome to demons and had such power, how much grace of the Spirit would living with him not have drawn down? For seeing Paul’s bed, seeing his mattress, seeing his sandals—would that not have been enough for them as a ground for continual compunction? For if demons shuddered when they saw his garments, much more did the faithful who lived with him feel compunction when they saw them. It is worth examining also why, in greeting them, he placed Priscilla before her husband. For he did not say, “Greet Aquila and Priscilla,” but “Priscilla and Aquila.” He did not do this without reason, but it seems to me he was aware of greater piety in her than in her husband. And that this is not guesswork can be learned from the Acts. For Apollos, a man who was eloquent and powerful in the Scriptures and knew only the baptism of John—she took him and instructed him in the way of God, and made him a finished teacher. For the women in the apostles' time did not busy themselves with the things women busy themselves with now: how to put on splendid clothes, how to beautify their faces with ointments and paints, choking their husbands and forcing them to buy a more expensive robe than the neighbor’s wife or the woman of equal rank, and white mules, and gold-studded bridles, and a retinue of eunuchs, and a great swarm of maidservants, and all the rest of the ridiculous display. But casting off all these things and throwing away worldly vanity, they sought one thing only: to become partners with the apostles and share in their same hunt.
orientation: Chrysostom is explaining why Paul stayed with Priscilla and Aquila for two years, comparing the apostles' search for worthy souls to rulers' search for splendid houses.

title: Women's teaching and the honor of hospitality
english: That is why she was not the only woman of this kind; all the rest were too. For about a certain Persis he says, “She labored much for us” (Romans 16:12), and he admires Mary and Tryphaena for these very labors, because they toiled alongside the apostles and stripped for the same contests. And how is it that when writing to Timothy he says, “I do not permit a woman to teach or to have authority over a man” (1 Timothy 2:12)? This is when the husband is devout, possesses the same faith, and shares the same wisdom. But when he is an unbeliever and has gone astray, he does not deprive her of the authority of teaching. At any rate, when writing to the Corinthians he says, “And if a woman has an unbelieving husband, let her not leave him. For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband?” (1 Corinthians 7:13, 16). And how would the believing woman save the unbelieving husband? By instructing him, clearly, and teaching him and leading him toward the faith, just as Priscilla did with Apollos. Besides, when he says, “I do not permit a woman to teach,” he is speaking about teaching on the platform, about public discourse, and about the kind that belongs to the priesthood; but he did not forbid private exhortation and counsel. For if it had been forbidden, he would not have praised this woman for doing it.

Let men hear, and let women hear these things too: the women, so that they may imitate their own kind and kinswoman; the men, so that they may not appear weaker than a woman. For what defense will we have, what pardon, when women display such eagerness and such discipline, while we are perpetually bound to the affairs of the world? Let rulers learn these things, and subjects, and priests, and those who hold the rank of the laity: the rulers, so that they may not admire the rich or chase after distinguished households, but seek virtue with poverty, and not be ashamed of the poorer among the brothers, nor pass by the tentmaker, the tanner, the purple-seller, and the bronze-worker to court those in positions of power. And the subjects, so that they may not think their circumstances are an obstacle to receiving holy people, but remembering the widow who received Elijah with only a handful of flour, and those who hosted Paul for two years, may they open their homes to those in need and hold all things in common with strangers.

Do not tell me, “You have no servants to wait on you.” For even if you have ten thousand, God commands you to harvest the fruit of hospitality through yourself. That is why Paul, speaking to a widow and commanding her to show hospitality, ordered her to do it not through others but through herself. For after saying, “If she has shown hospitality,” he added, “If she has washed the feet of the saints” (1 Timothy 5:10). He did not say, “If she spent money,” nor, “If she ordered her servants to do this,” but, “If she did this through herself.” That is why Abraham, though he had three hundred eighteen homeborn servants, ran to the herd himself, carried the calf, and performed all the other service himself, and made his wife a partner in the fruits of hospitality. That is why our Lord Jesus Christ was born in a manger, and after being born was raised in a house, and when he grew up had nowhere to lay his head (Matthew 8:20), so that through all things he might teach you not to gape at the splendid affairs of this life, but to be a lover of simplicity everywhere, to pursue poverty, to flee abundance, and to be adorned from within.
orientation: Chrysostom is explaining why Paul praised women like Priscilla for their labor, and is now answering an objection about Paul's command that women not teach.

title: True adornment is within; work is no disgrace
english: For all the glory of the king's daughter is within, he says (Psalm 45:13 LXX). If you have a hospitable disposition, you possess the entire treasury of hospitality, even if you own only a single obol. But if you are a hater of people and a hater of strangers, even if you are wrapped in every kind of wealth, your house is cramped for strangers. She did not have couches inlaid with silver, but she had abundant self-control. She did not have fine bedding, but she possessed a gentle and hospitable disposition. She did not have flashing columns, but she had a beauty of soul that shone forth. She did not have walls covered in marble or a floor adorned with mosaic stones, but she herself was a temple of the Spirit. These are the things Paul praised; these are the things he loved. For these reasons he stayed in her house for two years and would not leave. For these reasons he remembers them constantly and composes for them a great and wondrous encomium—not to make them more illustrious, but to lead everyone else to the same zeal and to persuade them to call blessed not the rich, nor those in positions of power, but the hospitable, the merciful, the lovers of humanity, those who show great kindness toward the saints.

Since we have learned these things from this greeting, let us demonstrate them through our own deeds. Let us not simply call the rich blessed, nor despise the poor. Let us not be ashamed of trades, nor consider work a disgrace—but rather idleness, and having nothing to do. For if working were a disgrace, Paul would not have pursued it, nor would he have taken pride in it, saying: For if I preach the gospel, I have no ground for boasting (1 Corinthians 9:16). What then is my reward? That when I preach, I may set forth the gospel of Christ without cost (1 Corinthians 9:18). And if a trade were a disgrace, he would not have commanded those who do not work not to eat (2 Thessalonians 3:10). For sin alone is a disgrace, and idleness is accustomed to give birth to it—not just one or two or three sins, but every kind of wickedness all at once. That is why a certain wise man, showing that idleness has taught all evil, says when speaking about household servants: Put him to work, so that he may not be idle (Sirach 33:28). For what the bridle is to the horse, work is to our nature. If idleness were good, the earth would produce everything unsown and unplowed. But it does nothing of the sort. In the beginning, God commanded the earth to bring forth everything unplowed; but now he has not done it that way. Instead, he has given laws to human beings to yoke oxen, to drag the plow, to cut the furrow, to cast down seeds, and to tend the vine and the trees and the seeds in many other ways, so that the occupation of work may draw the minds of those who labor away from every wickedness. From the beginning, then, to display his own power, he arranged for all things to spring up without our labors. Let the earth sprout forth the herb of grass, he says (Genesis 1:11), and immediately everything flourished. But after that, not so. Instead, he commanded that these things be brought forth from the earth through our own labors, so that you might learn that he introduced toil for our benefit and advantage. And hearing, In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread (Genesis 3:19), seems to be a punishment and a penalty, but in truth it is an admonition and a discipline, and a medicine for the wounds that came from sin.
orientation: Chrysostom is still expounding Paul's greeting to Priscilla and Aquila, now contrasting outward wealth with inner virtue and defending manual labor against the charge of shame.

title: Paul's manual labor as a boast, and the shame of idleness
english: For this reason Paul also worked constantly—not only by day, but even in the night itself. And he proclaims it, saying, “Working night and day, so as not to burden any of you” (1 Thessalonians 2:9). Nor did he pursue the work merely for pleasure and recreation, as many of the brothers do. Instead, he showed such toil in it that he was able to help others as well. “These hands,” he says, “served my needs and those who were with me” (Acts 20:34). A man who commanded demons, who was the teacher of the world, who had been entrusted with all the inhabitants of the earth, who cared with great diligence for all the churches under the sun, and for peoples and nations and cities—this man worked night and day, and did not catch even a small breath from those labors. But we, who do not undertake even a ten-thousandth part of his care—rather, we cannot even bring it to mind—we live in idleness continually. And what defense will we have, or what pardon, tell me? From this all evils have entered life: that many consider it the greatest dignity not to practice their own trades, and the worst accusation to appear knowing any such thing. Paul was not ashamed to handle an awl and sew hides at the same time as he conversed with people of rank. No—he prided himself on the matter, even while countless brilliant and distinguished people came to him. And not only was he not ashamed to do these things, but he publicly displayed his occupation in his letters as if on a bronze pillar. What he had learned from the beginning, he continued to practice afterward as well—even after being snatched up to the third heaven, after being carried away to paradise, after sharing unutterable words with God. But we, who are not worthy even of his sandals, are ashamed of the very things in which he exulted. Every day we sin, and we do not turn back, nor do we consider it a disgrace. But living from honest labors we flee as something shameful and ridiculous. What hope of salvation will we have, then, tell me? For the one who is ashamed should be ashamed of sin, and of offending God, and of doing anything improper—but in trades and work he should exult. For in this way we will easily cast out wicked thoughts through the occupation of the mind with work, and we will help those in need, and we will not trouble the doors of others, and we will fulfill the law of Christ, who said, “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35). For this reason we have hands: so that we may help ourselves, and so that we may contribute from our own resources everything in our power to those whose bodies are maimed. So if anyone continues in idleness, even if he is healthy, he is more wretched than those with fevers. For the sick have pardon from their weakness, and they may obtain mercy. But the idle, disgracing the good condition of their body, are rightly hated by all, since they both transgress the laws of God, and plunder the table of the weak, and make their own soul more worthless. For this is not the only terrible thing—that when they ought to feed themselves from their own home and resources, they trouble the houses of others—but also that they themselves become worse than everyone.
orientation: Chrysostom is addressing his congregation, contrasting Paul's tireless tentmaking with their own idleness and misplaced shame about manual work.

title: Idleness corrupts all things; work preserves them
english: For there is nothing, nothing at all, that is not destroyed by idleness. Water that stands still rots, but water that runs and wanders everywhere preserves its own virtue. Iron that lies idle becomes softer and more worthless, consumed by heavy rust, but iron that is in works is far more useful and more beautiful, shining forth no less than any silver. You could see untilled earth producing nothing healthy, but only wicked weeds and thorns and thistles and fruitless trees, while earth enjoying work abounds with cultivated fruits. And each of the things that exist, to speak simply, is corrupted by idleness and becomes more useful through its own work. Since we know all these things, and how great is the harm from idleness and how great the gain from work, let us flee the one and pursue the other, so that we may live the present life with dignity, and help those in need from our own resources, and by making our own soul better may obtain the eternal good things. May it be granted to all of us to attain these, by the grace and love for humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and power, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
On Aquila and Priscilla, and on not speaking evil of the priests of God. Homily 2.

Have you been taught to consider nothing in the divine Scripture incidental? Have you learned to examine carefully even titles and names and bare greetings written in the divine oracles? For I think that no one among the diligent will any longer endure passing over any of the words laid down in the Scriptures, whether it is a list of names, or a reckoning of years, or a bare greeting to certain people. But so that this correction may be made more secure, come, let us go through today what remains of the greeting to Priscilla and Aquila. And indeed its introduction has helped us not a little. For it taught us how great a good work is, and how great an evil idleness is, and what Paul's soul was like—how wakeful and full of care, making great provision not only for cities and peoples and nations, but also for each one of the faithful. It showed how poverty is no obstacle to hospitality, and that what is needed everywhere is not wealth and money but virtue and a disposition having piety, and that those who have the fear of God are more illustrious than all, even if they are brought down to extreme poverty. At any rate, we now count Priscilla and Aquila—tentmakers and manual laborers, living in poverty—more blessed than all the kings. Those in high rank and power are forgotten, but the tentmaker with his wife is sung everywhere throughout the inhabited world. And if they enjoy such glory here, consider how great the rewards and crowns they will be counted worthy of on that day. And even before that day, they have reaped no small pleasure and benefit and glory now, having lived with Paul for so long a time.
orientation: Chrysostom is concluding his argument that idleness destroys everything and work preserves it, then he transitions into the second homily on the greeting to Priscilla and Aquila.

title: The apostles' clothing seems to break Christ's command
english: For what I was saying before, I say again now, and I will not stop saying it: not only their teaching, not only their exhortation and counsel, but even the very sight of the holy ones carried great pleasure and benefit—even the adornment of their clothes, even the manner of their sandals. From this, you see, a great benefit has been brought into our own life: learning how far they went in using necessities. They not only did not exceed the measure of need, but sometimes they did not even have the full measure of need itself; they persevered in hunger and thirst and nakedness. And when Paul commanded the disciples, he said, "Having food and covering, with these we will be content" (1 Timothy 6:8). But about himself he appears to say, "To this present hour we hunger and thirst and are naked and are beaten" (1 Corinthians 4:11).

But what I was saying in between—and what came to my mind afterward—I must set before you, since it involves a great deal of inquiry. What is this? I was saying that even the adornment of the apostles' clothes provides us great benefit. But while I was saying these things, the law of Christ came to my mind, the law he laid down for them, saying, "Do not acquire gold, or silver, or copper for your belts, or sandals, or a staff for the road" (Matthew 10:9-10). Yet Peter appears to have sandals. At any rate, when the angel woke him from sleep and led him out of the prison, he says, "Put on your sandals, and wrap your cloak around you, and follow me" (Acts 12:8). And Paul, writing to Timothy, says, "Bring the cloak that I left in Troas with Carpus when you come, and the books, especially the parchments" (2 Timothy 4:13).

What are you saying? Christ commanded them not even to have sandals, and you have a cloak, and another has sandals again? Now if they were some of the ordinary people, some of those who did not always obey the Teacher, what was said would not be a question. But since these are the very ones who gave up their own lives, the leaders and first of the disciples, and they obeyed Christ in everything—and Paul not only did what was commanded but even leaped beyond the lines, for while Christ commanded living from the gospel, this man lived by his own hands, doing more than what had been ordered—it is truly worth asking why, though they obeyed him in everything, they seem here to transgress his law.

But they do not transgress it. And this discussion will be useful to us not only for the inquiry on behalf of those holy ones, but also for stopping up the mouths of the Greeks. For many who overturn widows' houses, strip orphans bare, wrap themselves in everyone's property, and behave no better than wolves, living from the labors of others—when they often see some of the faithful wearing more clothes because of bodily weakness, they immediately throw Christ's law at us and say these words: "Did not Christ command you not to have two tunics, or sandals? How then do you transgress the law laid down about these things?" Then, after laughing lavishly and guffawing, and shaming the brother, they leap away. So that this may not happen, come, let us stop up their shamelessness.
orientation: Chrysostom is defending the apostles against the charge that they disobeyed Christ's command to possess nothing, after having praised the very sight and clothing of the saints as beneficial.

title: The command was temporary and for the apostles only
english: Now, it would have been possible to be rid of them by saying just one thing. What is that? If you consider Christ trustworthy, then you are right to put these commands forward and press them against us; but if you do not believe in him, why do you put forward his laws? When you want to accuse us, Christ seems to you a trustworthy lawgiver; but when you ought to worship and admire him, you no longer have any regard for the common Lord of the world.

Still, so that they may not think we say this because we lack a defense, let us now go to the actual solution of the questions. What, then, will the solution be? If we see to whom, and when, and why Christ gave these commands. For we must not simply examine the words by themselves, but also the person, the occasion, the reason—all these things must be investigated with precision. If we look carefully, we will find that these commands were not given to everyone, but only to the apostles, and not to them forever, but only until a defined time.

How is this clear? From the very words spoken. For he called the twelve disciples and said to them: “Do not go on the road of the Gentiles, and do not enter a city of the Samaritans; go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. Heal the sick, cleanse lepers, cast out demons. You received freely; give freely. Do not acquire gold, or silver, or copper for your belts” (Matthew 10:5-9). See the Teacher's wisdom, how he made the command light. For first he said, “Heal the sick, cleanse lepers, cast out demons,” and gave them his grace abundantly; then he commanded these things, making that poverty easy and light by the abundance of signs.

It is clear not only from this that these commands were given to them alone, but also from many other places. For he punished those virgins because they had no oil in their lamps (Matthew 25:1-13), and he accuses others because they saw him hungry and did not feed him, thirsty and did not give him drink (Matthew 25:42). How, then, could someone who had no copper, no sandals, but only one cloak, feed another person, clothe the naked, or bring the homeless into his house?

Apart from these, the same thing will be clear and evident from another direction. When someone came and said, “Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?” and after he listed all the things of the law, the man, asking further, said, “I have kept all these from my youth; what do I still lack?” he says to him: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell your possessions and give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matthew 19:16-21). Yet if this were a law and a command, he should have said it first from the beginning, and made it a law, and placed it in the rank of a command—not introduced it as counsel and exhortation. For when he says, “Do not acquire gold or silver,” he speaks as one commanding; but when he says, “If you wish to be perfect,” he speaks as one counseling and exhorting. Counseling and legislating are not the same thing. The one who legislates wants what is commanded to happen by every means; but the one who counsels and exhorts also entrusts the choice of what is said to the judgment of the hearer, and makes the listener master of whether to accept it or not.
orientation: Chrysostom is answering the charge that Christians disobey Christ's command to possess nothing, and now begins to show that the command was given only to the apostles and only for a limited time.

title: Why Christ first forbade, then allowed possessions
english: This is why he did not simply say, “Go, sell your possessions,” so that you would not think the saying was a law. How did he say it? “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell your possessions” (Matthew 19:21)—so that you might learn that the matter lies in the judgment of the hearers. Now, that these things had been commanded to the apostles alone is clear from this. But we have not yet found the solution. For even if this was legislated for them alone, why is it that although they were commanded to have no sandals and no second tunic, one of them is found owning sandals, and another even has a cloak? What then should we say to this? That he did not leave even them under the necessity of these laws forever, but when he was about to go to the saving death, he released them from this legislation. Where is this clear? From the Savior’s own words. For when he was about to journey to the passion, he called them and said, “When I sent you out without a purse or a bag, did you lack anything?” They answered, “Nothing.” Then he said to them, “But now let the one who has a purse take it, and likewise a bag; and let the one who has none sell his cloak and buy a sword” (Luke 22:35-36).

But perhaps someone might say, “You have freed the apostles from the charges by what you have said, but the question remains: why did Christ legislate contrary things, at one time saying, ‘Do not acquire a bag’ (Matthew 10:9-10), and at another, ‘Let the one who has a purse take it, and a bag’?” Why then did he do this? In a manner worthy of his wisdom and his providence for his disciples. At the beginning he commanded these things so that by deed and experience they might receive the proof of his power, and having received it, might from then on have confidence to go out into the whole world. But once they had come to know his power sufficiently, he wanted them also to display their own virtue from within themselves, and not to be carried by him to the end, but himself to yield ground in many places and allow them to endure trials, so that they might not remain idle forever.

Just as those who teach swimming, at the beginning place their hands under their students and carry them with great care, but after the first, second, and third day they often withdraw their right hand from them and tell them to help themselves, and somewhere they even permit them to be dipped a little and to take in a great deal of salt water with their mouths—so Christ did with his disciples. At the beginning and in the first stages he did not allow them to suffer anything small or great, but he was present everywhere, walling them in, fencing them about, preparing everything to flow to them in abundance. But when they needed to display their own courage, he contracted the grace a little, urging them to accomplish many things by themselves.

For this reason, when they had no sandals, no belt, no staff, no copper coins, they lacked nothing. “Did you lack anything?” he says. They answered, “Nothing.” But when he commanded them to have a purse and a bag and sandals, they are found hungry and thirsty and going naked. From this it is clear that in many places he allowed them to face danger and be hard pressed, so that they might have some reward. This is something like what birds do with their young. As long as their wings are tender, they sit on the nest and keep them warm. But when they see that they have fledged and are able to cut the air, they first make them fly around the nest itself, then lead them farther out—at the beginning following and carrying them, but after that leaving them to help themselves.
orientation: Chrysostom is defending the apostles against the charge that they disobeyed Christ's command to possess nothing, and now explains why Christ later changed the command.

title: Christ trains the disciples like birds, then explains the sword saying
english: Christ did the same. He nourished the disciples in Palestine as in a nest, and when he had taught them to fly by being present and carrying them along, he finally let them fly out into the world, commanding them in many places to help themselves. That this is true, and that they might learn his power, he stripped them of everything, sent them with one garment, and commanded them to walk without sandals. We will know this clearly when we hear the very words. For he did not simply say to them, “Take a purse and a bag,” but he reminded them of what had gone before, saying, “When I sent you out without a purse or a bag, did you lack anything?” (Luke 22:35). That is, “Did not everything flow to you with abundance, and did you not enjoy great plenty? But now I want you to strive on your own. I want you to gain experience of poverty. For this reason I no longer hold you to the necessity of the former rule, but I permit you to have a purse and a bag, so that I may not be thought to work out your affairs through lifeless instruments, but you also may have your own discipline to display.”

But someone might say, “Would not the grace have appeared greater if they had remained that way to the end?” But they themselves were not yet so approved. For if they had gained no experience of affliction, no poverty, no persecution, no distress, they would have remained idle and sluggish. Now he wanted not only the grace to shine forth, but also the approvedness of those who obeyed to be displayed, so that afterward no one could say, “They contributed nothing of their own; everything came from God’s intervention.” God could have kept them in such abundance to the end, but he did not wish to, for many necessary reasons that we have often spoken of to your love. One reason is this; another, no less than this, is that they might learn to be moderate; a third, that they might not receive a glory greater than human. For these reasons, and many more than these, he allowed them to fall into many unexpected things, and he did not wish to leave them under the strictness of the former legislation, but he relaxed and loosened the tension of that discipline, so that their life might not become heavy and unbearable for them, if they were often left on their own and compelled to keep that strict rule.

Since it is necessary to make clear what is obscure in the passage before us, I must speak of this too. For after saying, “Let the one who has a purse take it, and a bag,” he added, “And the one who has no sword, let him sell his cloak and buy one” (Luke 22:36). What can this mean? Does he arm the disciples—he who says, “If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also” (Matthew 5:39)? He who commands us to bless those who revile us, to endure those who mistreat us, to pray for those who persecute us—does he then arm them, and with a sword alone? What sense could this have? For if it was necessary to arm them at all, it was necessary to acquire not only a sword, but also a shield and a helmet and greaves. And in any case, if he was going to manage such things in a human way, how many would not have laughed at the command? For if they had acquired ten thousand such weapons against so great an assault and plot of peoples, tyrants, cities, nations, what would the eleven have appeared to be? Could they even have heard the sound of a horse neighing? Would they not have been terrified at the mere sight of armies—they who had been raised among lakes and rivers and little boats? Why then does he say this? He wants to show the assault of the Jews, and that they are about to seize him.
orientation: Chrysostom is explaining why Christ first sent the disciples with nothing and later told them to take purse, bag, and sword, using the image of a bird teaching its young to fly.

title: The sword saying as a riddle for the coming plot
english: And this he did not want to say openly, but through riddles, so as not to disturb them again. So when you hear him say, “What you have heard in the ear, proclaim upon the housetops, and what you have heard in the dark, speak in the light” (Matthew 10:27), you do not suspect that he is commanding them to leave the narrow streets and the marketplace and preach on the housetops—for the disciples do not appear to have done this. Rather, “upon the housetops” and “in the light” hint at boldness, while “in the ear” and “in the dark” mean this: what you heard in one small part of the world, in one region of Palestine, sound it out everywhere on earth. For he did not speak to them in the dark or in the ear, but on high mountains and often in the synagogues.

So we must understand it the same way here. Just as there, when we hear “housetops,” we understood it differently, so here, when we hear “swords,” let us not think that he commanded them to possess swords, but that through the swords he hints at the present plot, and that he was about to suffer from the Jews what he did suffer. And this is clear from what follows. For after saying, “Buy a sword,” he added, “For what is written about me must be fulfilled: ‘I was reckoned among the lawless’” (Luke 22:36-37). And when they said, “Here are two swords,” not understanding what was said, he says, “It is enough” (Luke 22:38). Yet it was not enough. For if he wanted them to use human help, not only two or three, but not even a hundred swords would have been enough. But if he did not want them to use human help, then even the two were superfluous.

Still, he did not uncover the riddle. For he appears to do this in many places: when they do not understand what is said, he passes by and leaves it, entrusting the understanding of what was said to the outcome of events afterward. This is what he did elsewhere as well. For when speaking about his resurrection, he said something like this: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). And yet the disciples did not know what was said. And that they did not know, the evangelist noted, saying, “When Jesus rose, then they believed his word and the Scripture” (John 2:22). And again elsewhere: “For they did not yet know that he must rise from the dead” (John 20:9).

But the question has a sufficient answer. Let us bring our discussion to the remaining part of the greeting. What then is being said, and how did we get onto these things? We were blessing Priscilla and Aquila, because they lived with Paul, because they learned from him with precision even the manner of his clothing, the manner of his sandals, and everything else. From this our question was born. For we were asking why, when Christ forbade having anything at all except only a garment, they appeared to have sandals and a cloak. Then the argument showed that they were not breaking the law, but were keeping it very strictly in using these things. And we were saying these things not to train you toward an abundance of possessions, nor to urge you to acquire more than you need, but so that you may have an answer for unbelievers who mock our ways.
orientation: Chrysostom is explaining why Christ told the disciples to buy a sword, arguing that the command was a riddle pointing to the plot against him, not a literal instruction to arm themselves.

title: Poverty as freedom and the praise of Priscilla and Aquila
english: For Christ, when he dissolved the former law, did not command us to have houses, or slaves, or beds, or silver vessels, or anything else of that kind, but to be freed from the necessity of the things mentioned before. And Paul gave this same counsel when he said, “If we have food and coverings, we shall be content with these” (1 Timothy 6:8). For what is beyond our need ought to be spent on those who lack it—just as Priscilla and Aquila also did.

That is why Paul praises and admires them, and composes the greatest encomium for them. For after saying, “Greet Priscilla and Aquila, my coworkers in the Lord” (Romans 16:3), he also gives the reason for such love. What reason is that? “They laid down their own neck for my life,” he says (Romans 16:4). So is it for this that you love and cherish them, someone might say? Most certainly. Even if this alone were true, it would be a sufficient encomium.

For the one who saved the general would have preserved the soldiers; the one who delivered the physician from dangers brought the sick back to health; the one who snatched the pilot from the surge freed the whole ship from the waves. In the same way, those who preserved the teacher of the world and poured out their own blood for his safety were common benefactors of the world, since by their care for the teacher they preserved all the disciples.

But so that you may learn that they were like this not only toward the teacher, but also showed the same care for the brothers, listen to what follows. For after saying, “They laid down their own neck for my life,” Paul added, “to whom not only I give thanks, but also all the churches of the Gentiles” (Romans 16:4).

What are you saying? Tentmakers, poor manual laborers, who have nothing more than necessary food—all the churches of the Gentiles give thanks to them? And what great thing were these two able to do for so many churches? What abundance of money did they have? What greatness of power? What boldness before rulers?

They did not possess abundance of money or power among those who rule. But what they had was greater than all these things: noble eagerness and a soul arrayed for dangers with great abundance. For this reason they became benefactors and saviors of many. For the rich and fainthearted could not benefit the churches as much as those who live with poverty and have great souls.

And let no one think what is said is paradoxical. For it is true, and is shown by the facts themselves. The rich man has many handles by which he can be harmed. He fears for his house, for his servants, for his fields, for his money—that someone may take away any of these things from him. And being master of many things makes him a slave of many things.

The poor man, however, being well-girded and having laid aside all these handles, is a lion breathing fire. He has a noble soul, and rising up against all things he easily does everything that can benefit the churches—whether he must rebuke, or admonish, or endure countless burdens for Christ. And since he has once despised this present life, he does everything easily and with great facility. For what does he fear, tell me? That someone may take away his money? But this cannot be said.
orientation: Chrysostom is answering an objection about the apostles' possessions and now explains that Christ's command was about freedom from necessity, then praises Priscilla and Aquila as examples of poor tentmakers who benefited all the churches.

title: Poverty as the Source of Boldness
english: But what if he should be driven from his homeland? Every city under heaven is his homeland. But what if someone should cut off his luxury and his retinue? He has said farewell to all these things, and he lives as a citizen of heaven, pressing on toward the life to come. And if he must surrender his very soul and pour out his blood, he will not refuse. From this, such a man is more powerful and more resourceful than tyrants, kings, crowds, and everyone else. And so that you may learn that what I am saying is not flattery but truth: those who possess nothing are the ones most able to speak freely. How many rich men were there in the time of Herod? How many rulers? Who stepped forward? Who rebuked the tyrant? Who defended the laws of God when they were being violated? None of the wealthy did. But the poor and destitute man, the one who had no bed, no table, no roof—John, the citizen of the desert—he alone, foremost in all boldness, was rebuking the tyrant and exposing his adulterous marriage, and in the presence and hearing of all he pronounced the verdict that condemned him. And before him again, the great Elijah, who possessed nothing more than a sheepskin, alone rebuked that impious and lawless Ahab with great courage. For nothing so prepares a man to speak freely, and persuades him to be confident in all dangers, and makes him invulnerable and strong, as possessing nothing and having no entanglement of affairs. So if anyone wishes to possess great power, let him embrace poverty, let him despise this present life, let him consider death to be nothing. Such a man will be able to benefit the churches more than not only the wealthy and the rulers, but even those who reign as kings. For kings and the wealthy, whatever they do, they do from their money; but such a man has often accomplished many great things from dangers and from deaths. And as much as blood is more precious than all gold, so much better is this contribution than that one.

Such were these hosts of Paul, Priscilla and Aquila. They did not have an abundance of money, but they possessed a disposition richer than all wealth, expecting to die each day, living amid slaughter and blood, and bearing witness through all their time. For this reason our affairs flourished in those days, because the disciples were bound to their teachers in this way, and the teachers to their disciples in this way. For Paul speaks not only about these two, but also about many others. Writing to the Hebrews, the Thessalonians, and the Galatians, he bears witness to all of them of a great onslaught of trials, and he shows through his letters that they were being driven out and cast from their homeland, losing their property, and facing danger even to the point of blood. Their whole life was full of struggle, and they would not have refused even to have their own limbs mutilated for their teachers. Writing to the Galatians, he said: "I bear you witness that, if possible, you would have gouged out your eyes and given them to me" (Galatians 4:15). And he commends Epaphras, the one in Colossae, again for the same things, saying that he was sick near to death, and God had mercy on him—and not only on him, but also on me, so that I might not have sorrow upon sorrow (Philippians 2:27).
orientation: Chrysostom is continuing his praise of the poor man's freedom, now arguing that poverty makes one bolder than kings and tyrants, and citing John the Baptist and Elijah as examples.

title: The danger of slandering spiritual fathers
english: He said this to show that he would rightly grieve over the death of his disciple. And again he reveals his virtue to everyone, saying: "He came near to death, having disregarded his life, so that he might fill up your lack of service toward me." What could be more blessed than those people, and what more wretched than us? For they gave even their blood and their lives for their teachers, while we often do not dare to give even a bare word for our common fathers. When we hear them blasphemed and reviled, both by their own people and by strangers, we do not silence those who speak, we do not stop them, we do not rebuke them. If only we ourselves did not begin this slander! But as it is, one could see that not so many mockeries and insults come from unbelievers against the rulers as come from those who seem to be believers and are ranked among us. Will we still ask where such carelessness and contempt for reverence came from, when we are so hostilely disposed toward our own fathers? For there is nothing—nothing at all—that could destroy and ruin the Church, or rather, this cannot easily happen from any other source, except when disciples are not bound to their teachers, children to their fathers, and subjects to their rulers with great exactness. Then, if someone speaks evil of a brother, he is barred from the reading of the divine Scriptures. "Why do you take up my covenant in your mouth?" God says. Then, giving the reason, he added: "You sat and spoke against your brother" (Psalm 49:16, 20 LXX; Psalm 50:16, 20 Hebrew). But if you accuse your spiritual father, do you think yourself worthy to step onto the sacred threshold? How could that make sense? For if those who speak evil of father or mother die by death, what punishment will be worthy for the one who dares to speak evil of the one who is far more necessary and better than those parents? And does he not fear that the earth might split apart and utterly destroy him, or that a thunderbolt might come down from above and burn up his accusing tongue? Have you not heard what happened to the sister of Moses when she spoke against the ruler? How she became unclean and fell into leprosy, and endured the utmost dishonor? And though her brother pleaded and fell before God, she received no forgiveness. She had exposed that holy one as an infant, and had cooperated in his upbringing, and in arranging how the mother might become his nurse, so that the child would not be raised by a barbarian hand. And after that she led the women, just as Moses led the men, and shared in bearing all the dangers. And though she was the sister of Moses, she gained nothing from all these things to escape the wrath of God for her slander. But Moses, who had secured pardon for so great a people after that unspeakable impiety, fell down for his sister and asked for pardon, yet could not make God merciful. He was even rebuked severely—so that we might learn how great an evil it is to speak evil of rulers and to judge the lives of others. For on that day, God will judge us not only for the sins we have committed, but also for the judgments we have passed on others. And often a sin that is light by nature becomes grave and unpardonable through the sinner's judgment of another.
orientation: Chrysostom is contrasting the devotion of Paul's disciples with his own hearers' failure to defend their spiritual fathers, and now warns of the judgment on those who slander them.

title: The measure of judgment and the honor due to priests
english: Perhaps what I have said is unclear; so let me try to make it clear. Someone sinned, and he condemned another person committing the same sin with great severity. On that day he will draw upon himself not as much punishment as the nature of the sin demands, but far more, double and triple. For God will reckon to him the penalty not on the basis of what he himself sinned, but on the basis of what he harshly punished another person for sinning in the same way. And that this is true, I will make fully evident to you, as I promised, from things that have happened and come to pass. The Pharisee, although he himself had not sinned but had lived in righteousness and had many right deeds to speak of, because he condemned the tax collector—the robber, the greedy man, the most lawless—paid such a penalty as to be kept in store for a punishment greater than that man's. And if the man who himself had not sinned, but condemned with a mere word another man who was sinning and was notorious to all for his lawlessness, drew upon himself such a punishment, then we who sin many times every day and condemn the lives of others—lives not even evident or clear to anyone—consider how great a punishment we will undergo, how we will fall away from all pardon. For with the judgment you judge, he says, you will be judged (Matthew 7:2).

For these reasons I beg and urge and entreat you to depart from this wicked habit. For we will not harm the priests who are spoken of badly, not only if what is said is false, but even if it is true. Since the Pharisee did not harm the tax collector, but even helped him, although he was saying true things about him. But we will entangle ourselves in the utmost evils. Since the Pharisee thrust the sword against himself, and having received a fatal wound he departed. So that we may not suffer the same things, let us restrain the unbridled tongue. For if he did not escape punishment for speaking badly of the tax collector, what defense will we have, we who speak badly of our fathers? If Mary, having slandered her brother once, paid such a penalty, what hope of salvation is there for us, when every day we wash the rulers with countless revilings? Let no one say to me, 'But that was Moses.' For I will be able to say, 'And that was Mary.' But in another way, so that you may learn this very thing clearly—that even if the priests are liable to charges, it is still not lawful for you to judge their life—hear what Christ says about the Jewish rulers: The scribes and the Pharisees sit on Moses' seat; so do and observe whatever they tell you, but do not do according to their works (Matthew 23:2-3). And what could be worse than those men, whose zeal corrupted those being taught? But nevertheless he did not bring them down from their dignity, nor did he make them easy to despise by those under their rule. And very reasonably so. For if those under rule seized this authority, they would be seen deposing everyone and bringing them down from the judgment seat. Therefore Paul too, when he insulted the high priest of the Jews and said, God is about to strike you, you whitewashed wall; and do you sit judging me? (Acts 23:3), when he heard some rebuking him and saying, Do you revile God's high priest? (Acts 23:4), wishing to show how much respect and honor one must assign to rulers, what does he say? I did not know that he was God's high priest (Acts 23:5).
orientation: Chrysostom is explaining why judging others makes one's own sins worse, then turns to the duty of honoring priests even when they are blameworthy.

title: The honor due to priests, even unworthy ones
english: For this reason David, when he had Saul in his power—Saul who was acting lawlessly, breathing murder, and deserving of countless punishments—not only spared his life, but would not even utter a harsh word against him. And he gives the reason when he says, 'He is the Lord's anointed' (1 Samuel 24:6). And not only from this, but from another example as well, you can see from great abundance how far the one under authority must stand from correcting the affairs of priests. For once, when the ark was being brought up, some of those under authority saw it tilting and about to fall, and set it upright—and they paid the penalty on the spot, struck by the Lord and left dead. And yet they were doing nothing improper: they were not overturning the ark, but setting upright what was about to topple and fall. But so that you might learn from great abundance the dignity of priests, and how it is not lawful for one who is subject and in the rank of the laity to correct such things, he killed them in the midst of the crowd, striking fear into all the rest by the great excess of it, and persuading them never to approach the sacred precincts of the priesthood. For if each person were going to bring himself into the dignity of the priesthood on the pretext of correcting what is done badly, neither would a pretext for correction ever be lacking, nor would we be able to distinguish ruler from ruled, since everything would be mixed together.

And let no one think that I say these things because I have condemned the priests—for by the grace of God they display great gentleness in all things, as you yourselves know, and have never given anyone any handle—but so that you may learn that even if you had wicked fathers and burdensome teachers, it would not be safe or secure for you even then to slander and revile them. For if concerning bodily parents a wise man says, 'Even if he loses understanding, forgive him; for what will you give back to them, as they have given to you?' (Sirach 3:13; 7:28), much more must this law be kept concerning spiritual parents, and each person must busy himself with and examine his own life, so that we do not hear on that day, 'Hypocrite, why do you see the speck in your brother's eye, but do not notice the beam in your own eye?' (Matthew 7:3).

For it is the work of hypocrites to kiss the hands of priests in public where everyone can see, and to touch their knees, and to ask them to pray on their behalf, and to run to their doors when in need of baptism—but at home and in the marketplaces to deluge with countless reproaches those who are the cause and ministers of so many good things for us, or to tolerate others who reproach them. For if the father is truly wicked, how do you consider him a trustworthy minister of those awesome mysteries? But if he seems to you a trustworthy minister of those things, why do you tolerate others speaking evil of him, and do not silence them, or grow indignant, or show displeasure, so that you may receive a great reward from God, and praise from those very accusers? For even if they are insolent ten thousand times over, they will certainly praise you and approve your care for your fathers; just as, if we do not do this, everyone will condemn us—even those who speak evil themselves. And this is not the only terrible thing, but also that we will pay the ultimate penalty there.
orientation: Chrysostom is continuing his warning against slandering spiritual fathers, now giving Old Testament examples of the danger of correcting or dishonoring priests.

title: Self-judgment averts God's judgment
english: For nothing harms the churches as much as this disease. Just as a body not tightly bound by its network of sinews produces many sicknesses and makes life unlivable, so too a church not wrapped in the strong, unbreakable chain of love produces countless wars, increases the wrath of God, and becomes the occasion of many trials. So that these things may not happen, and so that we may not provoke God, increase our own evils, prepare an inexorable punishment for ourselves, and fill our life with much unpleasantness, let us turn our tongue to good speech, let us busy ourselves with our own life each day, and, entrusting the judgment of others' lives to the One who knows secrets with precision, let us judge our own sins. For in this way we will be able to escape the fire of Gehenna. Just as those who meddle in others' evils pay no attention to their own, so those who fear to pry into another's life will take great care of their own offenses. And those who reckon up their own evils, judging them each day and demanding an accounting from themselves, will find the Judge gentle at that time. Paul made this clear when he said, "For if we judged ourselves, we would not be judged by the Lord" (1 Corinthians 11:31). So that we may escape that verdict, let us leave everything else aside, busy ourselves with our own life, punish the reasoning that persuades us to sin, prick the conscience, and demand an accounting from ourselves for what we have done. For in this way, having made the burden of our sins light, we will be able to enjoy much forgiveness, pass through this present life with pleasure, and attain the good things to come, by the grace and love for humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom glory be to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.
orientation: Chrysostom is concluding the homily, warning that slander against spiritual fathers is a disease that harms the churches, and urging self-examination instead of judging others.
